title: Inquiry-Based Mathematics Education: a call for reform in tertiary education seems unjustified
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the debate over inquiry-based mathematics education (IBME) at the tertiary level and asks whether reform efforts promoting minimally guided, inquiry-based instruction are justified by evidence from the learning sciences. The authors critically synthesize research from cognitive science and educational psychology to evaluate claims that students learn mathematics better when they discover ideas for themselves, that inquiry promotes deeper conceptual understanding and transfer, and that inquiry classrooms better support equity.

The paper does not report a new empirical intervention study; instead, it reviews and interprets prior experimental and meta-analytic evidence on discovery learning, explicit instruction, worked examples, scaffolding, and related instructional designs. The context is undergraduate mathematics education, especially in the United States and broader Anglosphere reform efforts, though the review also draws on evidence from elementary science reasoning, high school mathematics, and related domains as adjacent evidence.

The authors conclude that the case for radical adoption of IBME is not supported. They argue that novices generally learn novel mathematics more effectively with explicit instruction and expert explanations than with unassisted discovery or minimally guided inquiry. They further contend that inquiry is not inherently better for conceptual understanding or equity, and that for high-element-interactivity material, instruction should begin with explicit teaching before moving to problem-solving or inquiry tasks.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative critical commentary/scoping review rather than an empirical evaluation. It synthesizes prior literature and cites effect sizes from other studies, but does not generate original data or directly test an intervention.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues strongly for explicit instruction over inquiry-based mathematics, but its own contribution is interpretive rather than an intervention effect. Because it summarizes prior evidence with some reported medium effects in cited studies (e.g., d=-0.38 for unassisted discovery vs explicit instruction), the broader evidence base suggests educational relevance, but this paper itself has no direct measured impact.
